lessons.title: Number System
lessons.keyRule: HCF is the largest common factor; LCM is the smallest common multiple. For positive integers a and b: HCF × LCM = a × b.
lessons.tip: When the question asks when repeating events meet again, think LCM. For splitting equal groups without remainder, think HCF.

lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.keyRule: Percent means per hundred. p% of N = pN/100. For percentage increase multiply by (100+p)/100; for decrease by (100−p)/100.
lessons.example: 20% of 450 = 90. Increasing 450 by 20% gives 540; reducing 450 by 20% gives 360.
lessons.tip: Successive percentage changes are multiplicative, not additive: +20% followed by −20% gives a net 4% decrease.

lessons.title: Ratio & Proportion
lessons.objective: Split a quantity in a given ratio
lessons.keyRule: When A:B = a:b and total T, the first share is T × a/(a+b). Equal ratios remain equal when both terms are multiplied by the same nonzero number.
lessons.tip: Convert units first if the terms are in different units, such as hours and minutes.

lessons.title: Averages
lessons.keyRule: Average of n values is their sum divided by n. Required total = average × count. For consecutive equally spaced numbers, the middle number is the average.
lessons.example: Average of 12, 18 and 24 is 54/3=18. If a fourth number 26 is added, average becomes (54+26)/4=20.
lessons.tip: A change of one observation by d changes the average by d/n.

lessons.title: Profit, Loss & Discount
lessons.objective: Base percentage on the correct value
lessons.keyRule: Profit% and loss% are calculated on cost price. Discount% is calculated on marked price. Selling price = cost price × (100±profit/loss%)/100.
lessons.example: CP=₹500 and profit=20% → SP=₹600. Marked price=₹800, discount=25% → SP=₹600.
lessons.tip: A discount and a profit percentage generally use different bases; do not mix them.

lessons.title: Simple & Compound Interest
lessons.keyRule: Simple interest SI = P×R×T/100 when rate R is annual and time T is in years. For annual compounding, amount A=P(1+R/100)^T, and CI=A−P.
lessons.example: P=₹2,000, R=5%, T=2 years: SI=₹200; annual CI=₹205.
lessons.tip: Unless the question specifies otherwise, a quoted interest rate is normally per annum. Convert months to years.

lessons.title: Time & Work
lessons.keyRule: If A finishes work in a days, A's daily work rate is 1/a. If B takes b days and they work together, time = ab/(a+b), assuming constant rates.
lessons.example: A takes 6 days, B 12 days. Together: (6×12)/(6+12)=4 days.
lessons.tip: Workers can have different rates. Do not average their individual completion times.

lessons.title: Speed, Time & Distance
lessons.keyRule: Distance = speed × time; time = distance ÷ speed. Convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18. Relative speed is the sum for opposite directions and difference for same direction.
lessons.example: 72 km/h = 72×5/18 = 20 m/s. A 200 m train travelling at 20 m/s passes a pole in 10 seconds.
lessons.tip: For a train passing a platform, include both train and platform lengths.

lessons.title: Mensuration
lessons.keyRule: Rectangle area = length × breadth; perimeter = 2(l+b). Square area = side². Circle area = πr² and circumference = 2πr.
lessons.example: A rectangle 15 cm by 8 cm has area 120 cm² and perimeter 46 cm.
lessons.tip: Write the required unit: area in square units and volume in cubic units.

lessons.title: Algebra
lessons.objective: Use inverse operations to solve equations
lessons.keyRule: To solve ax+b=c, subtract b from both sides and divide by a. Keep both sides balanced. Factor simple quadratics when possible.
lessons.tip: Substitute the solution into the original equation to check it.

lessons.title: Fractions & Decimals
lessons.keyRule: Add fractions by taking a common denominator. Multiplying fractions means multiplying numerators and denominators. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal.
lessons.tip: Cancel common factors before multiplying large numerators and denominators.

lessons.title: Data Interpretation
lessons.keyRule: For a table, identify the relevant year, unit and category before doing arithmetic. Change% = (new−old)/old ×100. Averages use all observations, not just endpoints.
lessons.example: Sales rise from 120 to 150. Growth = 30/120×100 = 25%.
lessons.tip: Check whether a bar graph starts at zero or uses a truncated axis.

lessons.title: Trigonometry Basics
lessons.keyRule: For angle θ: sinθ=opposite/hypotenuse, cosθ=adjacent/hypotenuse, tanθ=opposite/adjacent. Pythagoras: a²+b²=c².
lessons.example: In a 3-4-5 right triangle, opposite=3 and hypotenuse=5 gives sinθ=3/5.
lessons.tip: Confirm which side is opposite relative to the stated angle before choosing a ratio.

lessons.title: Elementary Statistics
lessons.keyRule: Arrange values before finding the median. Mode is most frequent. Range = maximum−minimum. For an even number of observations, median is the mean of the two middle values.
lessons.example: For 3,5,5,7,10: median=5, mode=5, range=7.
lessons.tip: Mean and median are different; one extreme value can move the mean far more than the median.

lessons.title: Number Series
lessons.keyRule: Check differences, second differences, multipliers, square numbers, cubes, and alternating sequences before guessing. An arithmetic progression uses a constant difference.
lessons.example: 3,7,11,15,? has common difference 4, so the next term is 19.
lessons.tip: Test your rule against every given term, not just the last two.

lessons.title: Alphabet Series
lessons.objective: Index letters from A=1 to Z=26
lessons.keyRule: Convert letters to positions when patterns are unclear. Look for +2, +3, alternating steps, reversals, or pairs read from both ends.
lessons.example: B,E,H,K,? uses +3 positions, so N is next.
lessons.tip: If a position exceeds 26 in a cyclic coding question, wrap back to A only when the rule indicates cyclic coding.

lessons.title: Coding-Decoding
lessons.objective: Find the exact letter and word transformation
lessons.keyRule: Check letter-by-letter shifts, reversals, digit substitutions, opposite alphabet and positional changes. A single example can sometimes admit multiple rules, so use all examples provided.
lessons.example: If CAT is DBU, each letter shifts forward by one; DOG becomes EPH.
lessons.tip: Never infer an unstated coding rule from unrelated examples.

lessons.title: Analogies
lessons.objective: Identify the relationship, not surface similarity
lessons.keyRule: For numeric analogy test squares, cubes, multiplication, differences and digit relationships. For word analogy test object-use, part-whole, synonym, antonym and category.
lessons.example: 4:16 :: 7:? is square mapping, so 49.
lessons.tip: The same transformation must work for both pairs.

lessons.title: Classification & Odd One Out
lessons.objective: Find the property shared by three options
lessons.keyRule: Inspect number parity, squares, primes, units, alphabet order and semantic categories. The odd option must violate a property that the other three share.
lessons.example: 16,25,36,50: 50 is not a perfect square.
lessons.tip: Check all three matching options before settling on an answer.

lessons.title: Blood Relations
lessons.keyRule: Translate every statement into a link such as parent, child, sibling or spouse. Distinguish maternal and paternal relations. Avoid assuming gender when it is not given.
lessons.example: A is father of B; B is mother of C. A is C's maternal grandfather.
lessons.tip: Write a simple family diagram to reduce confusion.

lessons.title: Direction Sense
lessons.keyRule: Take east as +x and north as +y. Opposite moves cancel. When a question asks straight-line distance, apply Pythagoras rather than adding path lengths.
lessons.example: Move 3 km east and 4 km north. Shortest displacement is √(3²+4²)=5 km.
lessons.tip: Question may ask final direction, total distance travelled or displacement: these are different.

lessons.title: Ranking & Order
lessons.keyRule: For a person counted from both ends, total people = left rank + right rank − 1. If total is given, opposite rank = total−known rank+1.
lessons.example: 11th from left and 16th from right → total 26.
lessons.tip: Subtract 1 because the same person appears in both rank counts.

lessons.title: Syllogism
lessons.keyRule: Use set inclusion rather than everyday assumptions. All A are B and all B are C guarantees all A are C. A statement about 'some' does not automatically imply all.
lessons.example: All roses are flowers; all flowers are plants → all roses are plants.
lessons.tip: Do not reverse 'all A are B' into 'all B are A'.

lessons.title: Venn Diagrams
lessons.keyRule: Use circles for categories. All A are B means circle A lies inside B; some A are B means an overlap; no A are B means disjoint circles.
lessons.example: All sparrows are birds and all birds are animals: nested circles Sparrow inside Bird inside Animal.
lessons.tip: Distinguish possibility from necessity when assessing conclusions.

lessons.title: Seating Arrangement
lessons.objective: Track fixed conditions before relative clues
lessons.keyRule: For a row, draw slots from left to right. For a circular table, choose a direction and be consistent about whose left/right is referenced. Lock in any known endpoint positions first.
lessons.example: Five people in a row: if P is at the left end and Q sits immediately right of P, write P Q _ _ _.
lessons.tip: Mark unresolved slots and avoid assigning positions without evidence.

lessons.title: Clock & Calendar
lessons.keyRule: For weekdays, reduce large day offsets modulo 7. In clocks, the minute hand moves 6° per minute and the hour hand 0.5° per minute.
lessons.example: If today is Monday, 17 days later is Thursday because 17 mod 7 = 3.
lessons.tip: Be careful whether the start day is counted as day zero.

lessons.title: Mathematical Operations
lessons.keyRule: Custom operators override the everyday meanings of their symbols. Substitute the given numbers and evaluate brackets first. Follow the rule in the question.
lessons.tip: Do not apply conventional meaning to a symbol that has been redefined.

lessons.title: Statement & Conclusion
lessons.keyRule: A valid conclusion must follow from all statements without adding an unstated fact. Words like all, some, none and only change the logical scope.
lessons.example: All trains in group X are electric. Therefore any member of group X is electric; no claim follows about trains outside X.
lessons.tip: A conclusion that is merely plausible is not necessarily established.
